chapters.title: Chapter 1: What History Means by a Cycle

lessons.title: The Classic Cycle Theories: Kitchin, Juglar, Kuznets, and Kondratiev

body.text: There is no single market cycle. There are several, running at different speeds on top of each other. The biggest booms and busts tend to arrive when more than one of them turns in the same direction at the same time.

children.text: Lesson 1.1 showed that the Sensex has risen over decades while swinging hard in between. Economists noticed the same pattern in prices, trade and production long before India had a stock index. Over roughly 70 years, from the 1860s to the 1930s, four of them each identified a cycle of a different length, driven by a different part of the economy. Their names still show up in research reports and fund manager commentary. You do not need to believe in any of them as a timing tool. You do need to understand the four engines they describe, because each one is visible in Indian markets today.

children.text: Kitchin: The Inventory Cycle (3 to 5 Years)

markDefs.definition: Goods a business has produced or bought but not yet sold, such as unsold cars at a dealer or finished goods in a factory warehouse.

children.text: Joseph Kitchin, a British businessman and statistician, studied US and UK data and found short cycles of about 40 months. His explanation was

. When demand picks up, shops and dealers order more to avoid running out, so factories raise production. News of the shortages travels slowly and orders overshoot. Warehouses fill up, orders get cut sharply, and production falls even though end demand has only slowed. The swing in factory output is much bigger than the swing in what customers actually buy.

Indian auto companies show this clearly. Manufacturers report wholesale numbers, meaning vehicles shipped to dealers, while dealers report retail sales to customers. When wholesales run well ahead of retail for several months, stock piles up at dealerships. In 2024 the Federation of Automobile Dealers Associations (FADA) repeatedly warned that passenger vehicle stock at dealers had climbed well above normal levels. The fix is always the same: manufacturers cut dispatches, and their reported sales and share prices can weaken even while customers are still buying.

body.text: Practical habit: when an auto company's monthly sales number looks strong, check whether it is wholesale or retail, and compare it with FADA's retail data for the same month. A gap that keeps widening is an early sign of a Kitchin-style correction.

children.text: Juglar: The Investment and Credit Cycle (7 to 11 Years)

Clément Juglar, a French physician turned economist, studied banking crises in France, England and the United States and published his findings in 1862. He was one of the first to argue that crises were not random disasters but a recurring phase of a longer cycle. The engine is business investment. In good years companies borrow to build factories, power plants and roads. Too much capacity gets built, returns fall, loans turn bad, banks stop lending, and investment collapses until balance sheets are repaired. India lived through one complete Juglar cycle in the two decades after 2003.

body.title: India's capex and credit cycle, 2003 to 2024

events.title: The boom
events.description: Companies borrow heavily to build power plants, steel mills, telecom networks and roads. Bank credit grows at well over 20% a year for several years. Infrastructure and capital goods stocks become market favourites.

events.title: The shock, cushioned
events.description: The Global Financial Crisis hits, but government stimulus and RBI rate cuts keep many projects going, so the investment cycle is delayed rather than ended.

events.title: Projects stall
events.description: Land, environment and fuel supply problems stall large projects. In 2014 the Supreme Court cancels over 200 coal block allocations. Heavily borrowed infrastructure companies struggle to service their debt.

events.title: The bad loans surface
events.description: The RBI's Asset Quality Review forces banks to recognise hidden bad loans. The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code arrives in 2016. Gross NPAs of banks rise above 11% of loans by March 2018. Companies such as Lanco Infratech end up in liquidation.

events.title: Repair
events.description: The corporate tax rate is cut in September 2019. Companies spend the next few years paying down debt rather than building, and banks clean up their books.

events.title: A new upswing
events.description: Government capital spending rises sharply, with ₹11.11 lakh crore budgeted for 2024-25. Bank gross NPAs fall below 3% by 2024. Capital goods, defence and railway stocks lead the market once again.

body.title: Spot the Cycle
body.question: An investor bought a large infrastructure developer's shares in late 2007, when order books were full and the company was borrowing heavily to expand. Which classic cycle best explains why the stock spent most of the next decade far below that price?
options: Kitchin, because dealers were holding too much inventory
Juglar, because the investment boom built too much capacity on borrowed money and ended in a bad loan cycle
Kuznets, because India's population stopped growing
Kondratiev, because infrastructure is an obsolete technology
body.explanation: This is the Juglar cycle: a credit-fuelled investment boom, followed by stalled projects, bad loans and years of balance sheet repair. The share price reflected the full cycle, not just the company's order book at the peak.

children.text: Kuznets: The Building and Population Cycle (15 to 25 Years)

Simon Kuznets, who later won the Nobel Prize in Economics in 1971, found longer swings of roughly 15 to 25 years in construction, population growth and migration. Buildings take years to plan and finish, and they last for decades, so when a construction boom overshoots, the excess supply can take many years to absorb. Real estate is the classic Kuznets asset. Indian residential property went through a long boom in the 2000s, then close to a decade of stagnation marked by unsold inventory, delayed projects, RERA in 2016, demonetisation and the IL&FS crisis of 2018, and then a sharp revival after COVID.

Kondratiev: The Long Wave of Technology (45 to 60 Years)

Nikolai Kondratiev, a Soviet economist, argued in 1925 that capitalist economies move in long waves of about half a century. The idea was politically dangerous, because it implied capitalism would recover from its crises rather than collapse. He was arrested in 1930 and executed in 1938. Later economists, most famously Joseph Schumpeter, linked these long waves to clusters of new technology: a breakthrough arrives, a long boom follows as the whole economy adopts it, and the wave fades as the technology matures and returns fall.

body.caption: The long waves, as commonly described (dates are rough and debated)

cells: Mill-made British cloth floods Indian markets
India's first passenger train runs from Bombay to Thane in 1853
Tata Iron and Steel Company is founded in 1907
Public sector heavy industry, then the Maruti 800 in 1983
Infosys lists in 1993 and Indian IT services become a global industry

body.text: Treat Kondratiev waves with the most caution of the four. Since the 1780s there have only been about five of them, far too few to prove a pattern statistically, and economists disagree on where each wave starts and ends. The idea is useful for thinking about which technologies are early or mature. It is useless for deciding whether to buy the Nifty next month.

children.text: Schumpeter: The Cycles Run on Top of Each Other

In his 1939 book Business Cycles, Joseph Schumpeter gave the Kitchin, Juglar and Kondratiev cycles their names and proposed that they run at the same time, one layered on top of another. He suggested roughly three Kitchins fit inside one Juglar, and roughly six Juglars inside one Kondratiev. The implication matters more than the exact ratios. When the shorter and longer cycles are rising together, you get unusually strong booms. When they fall together, you get unusually deep busts. When they pull in opposite directions, a strong short-term upswing can fizzle because a long-term downswing is working against it.

body.title: Stylised illustration: two cycles and their combined effect

children.text: This chart uses made-up, perfectly regular waves to show the mechanism, not real data. Look at years 2 to 3, where both cycles are rising and the combined line hits its high. Then look at year 11, where the shorter cycle is at its peak but the combined line is barely positive, because the longer cycle has already turned down. The deepest point, around years 15 to 16, comes when both are falling together. Real cycles are nowhere near this tidy, but the principle holds: the same short-term upswing feels very different depending on what the longer cycle underneath it is doing.

body.title: Schumpeter's Arithmetic
body.prompt: Take Schumpeter's rough ratios at face value: 3 Kitchin cycles make 1 Juglar, and 6 Juglars make 1 Kondratiev. If one Kitchin cycle lasts 40 months, how many years long is one Kondratiev wave?
body.explanation: One Juglar = 3 × 40 months = 120 months = 10 years. One Kondratiev = 6 × 10 years = 60 years. That sits at the top of the 45 to 60 year range usually quoted, which shows how loose these ratios are in practice.

children.text: What the Theories Get Right, and Where They Fail

columns.label: Useful for
points: Naming the engine behind a boom or bust: inventory, capex, property or technology
Remembering that different sectors run on different clocks
Asking whether a strong short-term trend is fighting a longer one
Spotting overbuilding and over-borrowing before the bust arrives
Reading research reports that talk about the capex cycle or the real estate cycle

columns.label: Not useful for
points: Predicting the exact year of a peak or trough
Treating the lengths as fixed, when real cycles stretch and shrink
Ignoring policy: RBI and government action can shorten or extend any cycle
Long-wave forecasts, which rest on only about five data points

body.title: Sort the Headlines
body.scenario: You read four headlines in the business section one morning: (A) "Dealers flag 70 days of unsold car inventory ahead of the festive season". (B) "Order inflows for L&T and other capital goods makers hit a record as private capex returns". (C) "New housing launches in Mumbai and Pune fall for the third year in a row as unsold stock piles up". (D) "Generative AI spending could reshape global productivity over the next two decades".
body.prompt: Match each headline to the classic cycle it best illustrates, and say in one line why.
body.modelAnswer: (A) Kitchin. It is about inventory built up at dealers, which usually leads to production cuts over the next few months even if customer demand is holding. (B) Juglar. It is about businesses committing to multi-year investment in plants and infrastructure, the engine of the 7 to 11 year investment and credit cycle. (C) Kuznets. It is about construction and real estate supply adjusting slowly over many years, the classic long building cycle. (D) Kondratiev. It describes a possible new cluster of general-purpose technology that could drive a decades-long wave, which is exactly the kind of claim that is easy to make and very hard to verify in advance.

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: The cycle driven by construction, real estate and population, lasting roughly 15 to 25 years, is named after the economist ___.
body.explanation: Simon Kuznets identified these long building and population swings in 1930. The Kitchin cycle is about inventory, the Juglar cycle is about investment and credit, and the Kondratiev wave is about technology.

cards.definition: 3 to 5 years. Driven by businesses building up and then cutting inventory. Proposed by Joseph Kitchin in 1923.
7 to 11 years. Driven by business investment in fixed assets and the credit that funds it. Proposed by Clément Juglar in 1862.
15 to 25 years. Driven by construction, real estate, population and migration. Proposed by Simon Kuznets in 1930.
45 to 60 years. Driven by clusters of new technology. Proposed by Nikolai Kondratiev in 1925. The least statistically proven of the four.
The cycles overlap. Booms and busts are largest when several cycles move in the same direction at once.
Wholesale is what a manufacturer ships to dealers. Retail is what dealers sell to customers. A growing gap signals inventory building up.

body.label: FADA: Monthly Vehicle Retail Data
body.description: The Federation of Automobile Dealers Associations publishes monthly retail sales and commentary on dealer inventory. Compare it with the wholesale numbers auto companies report to NSE and BSE to watch the inventory cycle in real time.

children.text: Look back at the four engines and you will notice that three of them, inventory, investment and real estate, depend heavily on borrowed money. That is no coincidence. The next lesson looks at the force that runs underneath almost every cycle: credit and interest rates.

points: Four classic cycles describe four different engines: Kitchin (inventory, 3 to 5 years), Juglar (investment and credit, 7 to 11 years), Kuznets (construction and population, 15 to 25 years) and Kondratiev (technology, 45 to 60 years)
India's capex boom from 2003 to 2008, the bad loan crisis that peaked in 2018, and the revival after 2021 form one complete Juglar-style cycle
Indian housing sales fell from about 3.4 lakh units in 2014 to about 1.4 lakh in 2020 in the top seven cities, then hit a record of about 4.8 lakh in 2023, a Kuznets-style swing
Schumpeter argued the cycles run on top of each other, so the biggest booms and busts come when several turn in the same direction together
Kondratiev waves rest on only about five observations and should be treated as a way of thinking, not as evidence
Cycle theories help you identify what is driving a boom or bust. None of them can reliably tell you when it will turn
